definition: AI slop, also known as slop content or simply slop, is digital content made with generative artificial intelligence that is perceived as lacking in effort, quality, or meaning, and usually produced in high volume to gain advantage, to earn money, or to deceive people.
details: It is a form of synthetic media usually linked to the monetization in the creator economy of social media and online advertising. Coined in the 2020s, the term has a pejorative connotation similar to spam. "Slop" was selected as the 2025 Word of the Year by both Merriam-Webster and the American Dialect Society. AI slop has been defined as "digital clutter", "filler content prioritizing speed and quantity over substance and quality", and "shoddy or unwanted AI content in social media, art, books [and] search results". Jonathan Gilmore, a philosophy professor at the City University of New York, describes the material as having an "incredibly banal, realistic style" that is easy for the viewer to process. The effect of increasing AI slop on the web has been likened to the increase in entropy as driven by the Second Law of Thermodynamics.

explainer.lead: AI slop is the flood of quickly made AI text, images, and videos that offers little substance but can still attract clicks, advertising revenue, or political attention. It matters because this material can crowd out careful work, spread misinformation, and make genuine content harder to find and trust.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a factory making thousands of toy pictures as quickly as possible, without checking whether they are useful, truthful, or interesting. AI slop is like that factory's output: computers produce huge amounts of content, and people post it hoping something will become popular or make money.
tiers.practitioner: The pattern can involve generating prompts with a tool such as ChatGPT, feeding them into an image model such as Midjourney, and posting the results at high volume on platforms including Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube. The main pitfalls are low-quality or nonsensical output, misinformation, misleading claims of authorship, and engagement incentives that reward quantity over usefulness.
tiers.paperLevel: Kommers et al., in an academic article published in January 2026, argue that AI slop has resisted formal definition and has no precise boundary with non-slop. They identify three prototypical properties: superficial competence, asymmetric effort, and mass producibility; they also describe variation in instrumental utility, personalization, and surrealism.

explainer.example: A medical student in India reported earning thousands of dollars each month from low-effort AI-generated images on Instagram and Fanvue. After an initial attempt failed, he created an AI influencer called "Emily Hart" and added MAGA rhetoric to appeal to conservative American men.

usedIn.name: Social-media monetization
usedIn.detail: Creators post AI images and videos on Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Fanvue to attract engagement and advertising revenue.

usedIn.name: Political campaigning
usedIn.detail: AI-generated content is used for content farming, attention-seeking, shitposting, and engagement farming.

usedIn.name: Online retail
usedIn.detail: Some retailers use generated flower images to sell seeds for plants that do not exist.

usedIn.name: Children's video
usedIn.detail: YouTube recommendations have included AI-generated videos presented as educational but containing nonsensical or inaccurate material.

explainer.intuition: Generative AI makes producing content extremely cheap, while social platforms can reward even a tiny chance of going viral. Together, those conditions encourage creators to publish enormous quantities of material with little checking, originality, or care.
howItWorks: A creator chooses a topic likely to attract engagement or serve a persuasive goal.
Generative AI rapidly produces text, prompts, images, or videos.
The creator posts many versions, often with minimal review.
A few successful posts can generate attention, followers, or revenue.
Repeated at scale, the material clutters feeds and search results.
explainer.whyItMatters: Monetization and engagement incentives can make low-quality generation profitable at enormous scale. The results include misinformation, distorted history, deceptive retail images, reduced credit for human artists, and additional moderation burdens for online communities.
misconceptions: Not all AI-generated content is slop; the label concerns perceived quality, effort, and meaning.
There is no precise, universally accepted boundary between slop and non-slop.
Slop is not always bizarre or surreal; some of it looks realistic and is easy to process.
